boxes.text: mc.live.gain~, mc.stereo~, and mc.dac~ do not use the MC Wrapper, but they are designed to work with MC Wrapper objects.

The two patchers below yield the same output. In the patcher on the right, the 4 instances of the tri~ object are all wrapped inside of the mc.tri~ object which outputs the 4 individual outputs on 4 separate channels of the multichannel signal.

The MC Wrapper creates 1 - 1024 instances of an audio object inside a single object box. Each instance can be controlled independently, or all instances can be controlled together. The wrapper takes multichannel signals and connects each instance internally.

@chans 4 tells the MC wrapper to create 4 instances of the tri~ object inside. The output of each individual instance will be on a separate channel in the output.

@values assigns arguments to each of the 4 instances.
Most audio objects in Max are available in MC through a special wrapper technology which gives the normal objects MC capabilities.

Use mc.sig~ 1 to monitor the busy map state -- it will output 0 when a channel is not busy.

For more information on busy maps check out the <link href=";max openhelp mc.noteallocator~">mc.noteallocator~</link> and  <link href=";max openhelp mc.voiceallocator~">mc.voiceallocator~</link> objects.

To optimize CPU usage, each object in the MC Wrapper can turn off processing when not needed via busy maps managed by the mc.noteallocator~ and mc.voiceallocator~ objects.

Two things to note:
1) @initialvalues can be used instead of @values if that's clearer
2) @values only sets the first initial value of an object; if the object takes multiple typed-in arguments you cannot set the second or third ones with @values
Additional channels not in the @values list are set to the object's default value (in this case 0)
This is equivalent to making sig~ 1, sig~ 2, sig~ 3, and sig~ 4
Use @values to assign individual values to wrapper instances as typed-in arguments. Note that @values does not replace the need to specify how many channels / instances are in the object.
The applyvalues message and the @values attribute permit you to set values or attributes of MC Wrapper instances using lists. Each element in the list sets a successive instance.
applyvalues: Setting Instance Values in One Message
The applyvalues message is a way to send one value from a list to each individual instance; it works in any inlet and always applies the first value to the first instance

Each object using the MC Wrapper will have a number of instances specified by the @chans attribute. Unlike most attributes in Max @chans is not entirely dynamic.
@bz is an abbreviation for the @usebusymap attribute
turn @zero off to stop clearing unused signal memory of the wrapper objects (mc.tri~, mc.*~, and mc.line~)
turn metro on to start beautiful melody
repeatedly toggle this on and off to manipulate the busy map of mc.voiceallocator~ leaving remnants of old signal data around
this meter shows the effect of turning @zero off and then toggling the mc.sig~ above for unused channels -- channels will be "frozen" with data in them when not in use
if you turn this off after disabling @zero, you risk hearing loud noise (observe the meter~ monitoring the "noise" level above)

By default, when a channel of an MC Wrapper object is not in use due to the busy map, it outputs a constant zero. You can save even more CPU by turning the zero output off, but you risk loud noise due to the presence of garbage in the internal signal buffers, so you need to manage this carefully. The mc.stereo~ object (mc.stereo~ is a two-channel version of mc.mixdown~) uses the busy map by default and will not mix this garbage output to your speakers.

The exponential and scaledexponential messages define an exponential range using the argument as the exponent

the range will be generated over the space of five channels

Use the spread message and its variants to generate linear ranges of values over the space of instances inside the wrapper. Or use exponential and scaledexponential messages to generate exponentially scaled ranges.
The "spread" message will define a range of values based on its two arguments. This range is then divided evenly and the values are sent to the individual instances in the wrapper.
Connect a multichannel signal to jit.cellblock to see the values in each channel.
see the generated values by looking at an mc.sig~ object with the same number of channels connected to a visualizer such as jit.cellblock
The deviate and increment messages work with attributes too:
Note that while these messages are quick to use, it's not easy to see the values they produce. See an example using mc.sig~ and jit.cellblock below.

The deviate message applies randomly generated values to all MC Wrapper instances. It's one of a family of features the wrapper has for generating "spaces" of values across channels and instances. The increment message generates a range by adding a value to each successive channel.
set the amount of the increment for each channel (0 is no increment), for example an increment of 9 would be 1000, 1009, 1018, 1027 etc.

The setvalue message allows you to target an individual instance within the wrapper. Any message following setvalue and an instance number sends that message to the instance.
setvalue: Changing the values of individual instances
regular Max messages set all values identically
You can set the values of all MC Wrapper instances together, or set the values of individual instances.
regular typed-in arguments set all values identically
